title: Revelation: When History Comes Together
scripture: Revelation 11:4–12; Exodus 7:14–25; 1 Kings 17:1; Daniel 7:25; Ezekiel 37:1–14; Zechariah 4:1–14.
theme: The history hidden within the symbols of Revelation
opening: Across the centuries as established in Revelations
prayer: Lord, open our minds and hearts to the history of Your Word. Help us recognize the connections we have overlooked and understand more of what You have revealed. Give us humility before what remains mysterious and a greater desire to continue discovering You through Scripture. Amen.
body:
The Book of Revelation can be difficult to understand. We encounter beasts, strange numbers, extraordinary powers, and visions that seem almost impossible to explain. Yet much of what John describes is rooted in events that occurred hundreds of years earlier. Today's reading, Revelation 11:4–12, offers a remarkable example.

John describes two witnesses who can prevent rain from falling, turn water into blood, and strike the earth with plagues. They cannot be destroyed until they have finished their testimony. Then a beast rises from the abyss, overcomes them, and kills them. Their bodies are left unburied in the street of a great city. For three and a half days, people from different nations look upon them. Rather than mourning, they rejoice and exchange gifts because these prophets had tormented the inhabitants of the earth. These people do not regard the witnesses as servants of God. They regard them as tormentors whose deaths deserve celebration. But John has already identified them as God's witnesses.

How could the same people be understood so differently? And why does John describe their powers and deaths in such unusual language? To understand, we need to travel backward through the history of Israel.

The story begins with Moses, who led the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt. In the Book of Exodus, Pharaoh refuses to release the Israelites despite repeated warnings. God works through Moses and Aaron, bringing plagues upon Egypt. One of these turns the waters of the Nile into blood. To the enslaved Israelites, Moses is the man through whom God is bringing liberation. To Pharaoh, Moses is a threat to his authority and to the kingdom he rules. The same actions that bring hope to one people bring judgment upon another. Now consider Revelation. John's witnesses possess the power to turn water into blood and strike the earth with plagues. The resemblance to Moses is our first historical clue.

Generations after Moses, the Israelites established a monarchy. Saul became their first king, followed by David and then Solomon. Under David and Solomon, the tribes were united under one kingdom. Jerusalem became the capital, and Solomon built the first Temple there. But after Solomon's death, around 930 BC, the kingdom divided. The northern kingdom retained the name Israel, while the southern kingdom became Judah, with Jerusalem remaining its capital. This division shaped the history of the prophets who followed. They were often sent to confront rulers who claimed authority over God's people but had turned away from His commandments.

One of those prophets was Elijah. He lived in the northern Kingdom of Israel during the ninth century BC, under King Ahab. Ahab and his wife Jezebel promoted the worship of Baal, a Canaanite deity associated with storms and fertility. Elijah challenged this worship and called Israel back to the Lord. In 1 Kings 17, Elijah announced that rain would cease except at his word. This is another power possessed by the witnesses in Revelation.

But something else happens in Elijah's story that is especially important. When King Ahab encounters Elijah in 1 Kings 18:17, he asks, “Is it you, you disturber of Israel?” Ahab believes Elijah is responsible for the suffering of the kingdom. Elijah answers that it is Ahab who has brought trouble upon Israel by abandoning God's commandments and following Baal. The king regards God's prophet as the enemy of his people, while the prophet identifies the king's disobedience as the source of their trouble. Both see the same suffering, but they understand its cause very differently.

Centuries later, John's two witnesses are also regarded as tormentors. When they die, the people celebrate. And yet they belong to God. Moses and Elijah are not explicitly named as the witnesses in Revelation, but their powers and experiences are woven into John's description. Both confronted rulers who resisted God's message, and both became sources of trouble to those unwilling to receive it. Moses and Elijah also appear together with Jesus at the Transfiguration, connecting the Law and the Prophets with Christ.

After Elijah's lifetime, the kingdoms of Israel and Judah continued to experience political instability and conflict. In 722 BC, the Assyrian Empire conquered the northern Kingdom of Israel. Many inhabitants were displaced, and the northern kingdom ceased to exist as an independent state. Judah survived for more than another century, but Babylon eventually became the dominant power in the region. In 597 BC, Babylon captured Jerusalem and deported King Jehoiachin along with many priests, officials, and skilled inhabitants. Among those taken into exile was Ezekiel. In 586 BC, the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem and Solomon's Temple.

The Jewish people had lost their political independence, their Temple, and, for many, their homeland. Their national and religious identity had been shaken. It was during this period of upheaval that Ezekiel received some of the most extraordinary visions in Scripture.

Ezekiel was both a priest and a prophet. He began his ministry among the exiles in Babylon around 593 BC. His early prophecies warned of Jerusalem's coming destruction. After the city fell, his message increasingly turned toward restoration. In Ezekiel 37, God brings him into a valley filled with dry bones. The bones represent the people of Israel, who believe their hope has perished. God commands Ezekiel to prophesy over the bones. They come together, flesh covers them, but they remain lifeless. Then breath enters them, and they stand upon their feet. God explains that He will restore His people, who have come to believe that their future is gone.

Now consider Revelation 11:11: *“But after the three and a half days, a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood on their feet.”* John's words recall Ezekiel's vision. Ezekiel describes the restoration of Israel after national devastation. John describes the restoration of two witnesses after their enemies have celebrated their deaths. The events are different, but the imagery is closely connected.

Daniel's story is also set during the Babylonian exile, although the Book of Daniel reached its final form centuries later, during the second century BC, when Jewish people were again suffering persecution. Daniel's visions describe powerful kingdoms, terrifying beasts, and rulers who persecute God's people. In Daniel 7:25, one persecuting power is permitted to prevail for “a time, two times, and half a time.” One plus two plus one-half equals three and a half.

Why does this matter? Throughout Scripture, seven frequently represents fullness or completion. The creation account culminates in the seventh day. Revelation repeatedly uses seven: seven churches, seven seals, seven trumpets, and seven bowls. Three and a half is half of seven. In Daniel and Revelation, this number becomes associated with a limited period of persecution or suffering.

John repeats the pattern in several forms. In Revelation 11:2, the holy city is trampled for **42 months**. In Revelation 11:3, the witnesses prophesy for **1,260 days**. Using a symbolic calendar of thirty-day months, both periods equal three and a half years. Then the witnesses lie dead for **three and a half days**. The periods are not necessarily describing identical events, but John is using the numerical language already found in Daniel. The people celebrating the witnesses' deaths believe their victory is complete. Yet the three and a half days come to an end.

There is another unusual description in Revelation 11:4. John calls the witnesses *“the two olive trees and the two lampstands.”* This imagery comes from Zechariah, a prophet who lived after the Babylonian exile. When Persia conquered Babylon in 539 BC, the Persian king Cyrus permitted Jewish exiles to return to their homeland. Jerusalem had been devastated, and the Temple needed rebuilding. Around 520 BC, Zechariah encouraged the returning community during this difficult period.

In Zechariah 4, he describes a golden lampstand and two olive trees that supply oil to it. The two anointed figures are traditionally understood as Joshua, the high priest, and Zerubbabel, the governor, who were involved in rebuilding the community and its Temple. The central message of the vision is: *“Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, says the LORD of hosts.”* The olive trees provide the oil that sustains the lamp's light. The vision emphasizes that God's work depends upon His Spirit rather than human strength. John takes up this image when describing his witnesses. Earlier, in Revelation 1:20, Jesus had identified lampstands as symbols of churches.

John writes Revelation in the first century after Christ, drawing upon a history that stretches across many centuries. Moses confronted Pharaoh in Egypt, and water turned to blood. Elijah confronted Ahab in the divided Kingdom of Israel, announced a drought, and was accused of bringing trouble upon his people. Ezekiel, exiled after Babylon conquered Jerusalem, envisioned God's breath restoring life to those who appeared beyond hope. Daniel described kingdoms, persecution, and a mysterious period of three and a half. Zechariah, living after the exile, saw olive trees supplying a lampstand and heard God's promise that His work would be accomplished through His Spirit.

John gathers these images into the account of two witnesses. Their powers recall Moses and Elijah. Their description recalls Zechariah. The duration of their apparent defeat recalls Daniel. Their restoration to life recalls Ezekiel.

And the people's reaction recalls something we have already encountered in Israel's history. Pharaoh resisted Moses. Ahab accused Elijah of troubling Israel. In Revelation, the people celebrate the deaths of God's witnesses because they believe those witnesses were their enemies.

For three and a half days, they look upon the bodies and rejoice. But the witnesses had not been acting on their own authority. John had told us from the beginning that they belonged to God and that their mission would continue until their testimony was finished.

Then, before the people who had celebrated their deaths, the breath of life from God enters them. They stand upon their feet. And a voice from heaven calls them upward.
